Common periwinkle populations in the intertidal zone along European coastlines exhibit remarkably consistent growth trajectories across their range. Field surveys indicate that newly settled individuals possess a shell height at settlement of approximately 3 millimeters , a diminutive size that reflects the challenges of locating suitable microhabitats within the first weeks of benthic life. In contrast, the ultimate shell height documented for this species reaches 3.8 centimeters [Li = 3.8 centimeters], a terminal size that is among the largest recorded for littorinids occupying similar wave-exposed shores. This span from less than half a centimeter to nearly four centimeters in shell length constitutes an extraordinary scope of post-metamorphic growth, one that is sustained across a broad thermal gradient. Laboratory rearings conducted at a constant water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] have demonstrated that the time since birth at settlement is 152.5 days , a protracted interval that suggests delayed metamorphosis under cooler thermal regimes. Such prolonged planktonic duration may enhance dispersal potential but simultaneously increases vulnerability to pelagic predation before the critical transition to a demersal existence.

Female reproductive maturation in this gastropod follows a distinct schedule that has been characterized in both field collections and controlled laboratory experiments. Coastal populations monitored in the Gulf of Maine exhibit shell height at puberty for females of 1.1 centimeters [Lp = 1.1 centimeters], a body size that correlates closely with the onset of gonadal activity and the first deposition of egg capsules on hard substrates. Under stable thermal conditions maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been measured at 549 days [tp = 549 days], indicating that almost eighteen months elapse from hatching before an individual reaches the reproductive stage of its life cycle. This relatively delayed maturation is likely attributable to the energetic demands of constructing the robust, thick-walled shell that provides crucial defense against crushing predators such as the green crab Carcinus maenas. The pronounced variability observed in both size and age at maturity across populations suggests that local food availability and thermal history exert considerable influence on the pace of somatic development in Littorina littorea.

Reproductive output in this oviparous mollusc is initiated with the production of minute, planktonically-dispersed eggs that are encapsulated in gelatinous masses attached to submerged rock surfaces. Each fertilised ovum begins its development with an egg dry weight of just 0.000001376 grams , an extraordinarily low maternal investment per offspring that is typical of species producing large numbers of propagules to offset high larval mortality in the water column. This dry mass is among the lowest recorded for any littorinid species and suggests a strategy that prioritizes numerical fecundity over per-offspring provisioning. The gelatinous matrix surrounding these eggs provides a measure of protection against desiccation during low tide and against micro-invertebrate predators, though the tiny individual embryos remain highly vulnerable to environmental extremes. Gravid individuals have been observed depositing hundreds of these capsules during a single reproductive period, and the cumulative annual output represents a substantial investment of somatic resources toward gamete production in this iteroparous grazer.

Feeding ecology in the common periwinkle is dominated by the consumption of intertidal macroalgae, particularly the green alga Ulva lactuca, which forms dense mats on mid-intertidal benches. Measurements of mass-specific food intake derived from Ulva lactuca assays indicate that the specific feeding rate at 0.3 grams dry weight is 190.8 joules per day per gram  and was determined at an experimental temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This value corresponds to approximately 45.6 calories of Ulva consumed per gram of periwinkle dry mass each day, revealing a substantial ingestion rate that supports the species' rapid juvenile growth phase. The radular structure of Littorina littorea is well-adapted to rasping the thallus surface of fleshy algae, and field observations confirm that grazing intensity increases markedly during periods of warm water temperature when metabolic demands are elevated. The availability of Ulva beds directly influences local population density, as periwinkles congregate in areas of high algal cover, and competition for preferred food patches can be intense among size-classes occupying the same tidal height.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 2190 days [am = 2190 days] when individuals are maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a duration that is relatively extended for an intertidal gastropod of this body size and likely reflects the protective benefits of its robust shell against wave dislodgment and crushing by predators. Senescence in older individuals is typically marked by a progressive thinning of the shell margin, increased epibiont fouling by barnacles and bryozoans, and a measurable decline in the maximum daily feeding rate as radular teeth become worn from decades of continuous grazing on abrasive algal and microbial films. Populations inhabiting the uppermost reaches of the intertidal zone, where thermal and desiccation stress are greatest, often exhibit reduced average lifespans compared with conspecifics from lower, more consistently submerged zones, yet a small proportion of individuals in every cohort still reach the age-related mortality boundary of roughly six years. The combination of protracted maturation, extended reproductive lifespan, and high fecundity per spawning event allows this species to maintain dense populations across a wide latitudinal gradient.
